nodes.label: Fluid Mechanics
nodes.note: Hydrostatics, buoyancy, Bernoulli flow, viscosity, and surface tension. Watch for the three disguises of one idea: force balance, energy per volume, and pressure gradients.

nodes.label: Fluid Statics and Pressure
nodes.note: Pressure at rest, Pascal's law, hydrostatic variation, and liquids in accelerated frames. Statics means no shear: pressure is isotropic.

nodes.label: Pressure Definition
nodes.note: Pressure is normal force per unit area: $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$, in pascals (N/m$^2$). In a static fluid it acts equally in all directions at a point.

nodes.label: Pascal's Law and Hydraulics
nodes.note: An applied pressure transmits undiminished through the fluid: $$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$. Hydraulic lifts trade distance for force by a factor $A_2/A_1$.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic Variation
nodes.note: Pressure grows linearly with depth: $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$. Shape of the container is irrelevant; only the depth of the free surface matters.

nodes.label: Accelerated Container
nodes.note: In a frame accelerating horizontally the free surface tilts: $$\tan\theta = \frac{a}{g}$$. Effective gravity becomes the vector sum $\vec{g} - \vec{a}$.

nodes.label: Rotating Liquid Column
nodes.note: Steady rotation makes the surface a paraboloid: $$z = \frac{\omega^2 r^2}{2g}$$. The pressure gradient balances both gravity and centrifugal acceleration.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic Paradox
nodes.note: The force on the base of a vessel is $$F = \rho g h\, A$$, regardless of the vessel's shape or the total volume of water. Containers of different shapes with the same base and fill height push down with equal force.

nodes.label: Buoyancy and Flotation
nodes.note: Archimedes' principle, apparent weight, floating equilibrium, and buoyancy in non-inertial frames. Weight minus upthrust is what a spring balance reads.

nodes.label: Archimedes' Principle
nodes.note: Upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid: $$F_B = \rho_f V_{sub} g$$. It depends on the fluid and submerged volume, never on the object's material.

nodes.label: Apparent Weight
nodes.note: Immersion reduces the measured weight: $$W_{app} = W - F_B = (\rho_{obj} - \rho_f) V g$$. A body denser than the fluid still sinks but weighs less.

nodes.label: Flotation Condition
nodes.note: A floating body displaces its own weight: $$\rho_{obj} V_{obj} = \rho_f V_{sub} \Rightarrow \frac{V_{sub}}{V_{obj}} = \frac{\rho_{obj}}{\rho_f}$$. Ice floats with about 92% of its volume below water.

nodes.label: Floating Ice Melting
nodes.note: Since the displaced water volume equals the water the ice will form, the level in the glass is unchanged: $$V_{disp} = \frac{m_{ice}}{\rho_w}$$. Adding salt or alcohol changes the answer.

nodes.label: Buoyancy in Accelerated Frames
nodes.note: Replace g by the effective gravity: $$F_B = \rho V (g \pm a)$$. In free fall, buoyancy and apparent weight both vanish.

nodes.label: Fluid Dynamics and Bernoulli
nodes.note: Ideal flow, continuity, Bernoulli's theorem, and efflux applications. Energy conservation per unit volume is the master key.

nodes.label: Ideal Fluid Assumptions
nodes.note: Ideal flow is incompressible, non-viscous, and irrotational: $\nabla \cdot \vec{v} = 0$ and streamlines never cross. Real problems assume this before corrections.

nodes.label: Gauge vs Absolute Pressure
nodes.note: Instruments read gauge pressure above atmosphere: $$P_{gauge} = P - P_{atm} = \rho g h$$. Hydrostatic problems inside open tanks use gauge pressure unless stated otherwise.

nodes.label: Equation of Continuity
nodes.note: Mass conservation for incompressible flow: $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$. Where the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up.

nodes.label: Bernoulli's Theorem
nodes.note: Energy per unit volume is conserved along a streamline: $$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = const$$. Fast streamlines carry low pressure (Venturi effect).

nodes.label: Venturimeter
nodes.note: Measuring two pressures across a contraction yields the flow speed: $$v_2 = A_1\sqrt{\frac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho(A_1^2 - A_2^2)}}$$. Continuity plus Bernoulli convert pressure difference into discharge.

nodes.label: Torricelli's Law
nodes.note: Efflux speed from a small hole at depth $h$: $$v = \sqrt{2gh}$$. The emerging jet follows projectile motion from the orifice.

nodes.label: Range of the Efflux Jet
nodes.note: A horizontal jet from a hole at depth $y$ below the surface of a tank of height $H$ lands at $$R = 2\sqrt{y\,(H - y)}$$. Maximum range $2H$ occurs for a hole at mid-depth $y = H/2$.

nodes.label: Hydraulic Press Force
nodes.note: Pascal multiplication gives the press force: $$F_2 = F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1}$$, while the work input equals work output since $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$. A press multiplies force, not energy.

nodes.label: Viscosity and Fluid Friction
nodes.note: Newton's law of viscosity, Poiseuille flow, Stokes drag, and the Reynolds number. Dissipation enters only when layers slide.

nodes.label: Newton's Law of Viscosity
nodes.note: Shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient: $$F = \eta A \frac{dv}{dy}$$. Coefficient $\eta$ (Pa.s) measures internal friction.

nodes.label: Poiseuille's Law
nodes.note: Laminar discharge through a capillary: $$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \eta L}$$. The $R^4$ dependence makes small changes in radius dominant.

nodes.label: Stokes' Law
nodes.note: Drag on a sphere at low speed: $$F = 6\pi \eta r v$$. Opposing weight and buoyancy this gives terminal velocity.

nodes.label: Terminal Velocity
nodes.note: Balancing Stokes drag with net weight: $$v_t = \frac{2 r^2 (\rho_s - \rho_f) g}{9 \eta}$$. It scales with the square of the drop radius.

nodes.label: Drag Regimes
nodes.note: At low Reynolds number drag is viscous and linear, $F \propto v$ (Stokes); at high Reynolds number it is inertial and quadratic, $F = \tfrac{1}{2} C_d \rho A v^2$. Terminal speed follows from setting drag equal to weight in the right regime.

nodes.label: Temperature and Viscosity
nodes.note: Liquid viscosity falls rapidly with temperature, roughly $$\eta \propto e^{E_a/RT}$$ (Andrade), while gases get more viscous as they warm. Heating honey makes it pour faster; heating air thickens its internal friction.

nodes.label: Reynolds Number
nodes.note: The dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces is $$R_e = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$$. Flow is laminar below $\sim 2000$ and turbulent above $\sim 4000$ in pipes.

nodes.label: Surface Tension and Capillarity
nodes.note: Surface energy, excess pressure in curved interfaces, contact angle, and capillary rise. Molecular cohesion at the free surface, made measurable.

nodes.label: Surface Energy
nodes.note: Creating area costs energy: $$W = \sigma \Delta A$$, so surface tension $\sigma$ (N/m) is energy per unit area. Liquids minimise surface area into spheres.

nodes.label: Young-Laplace Pressure
nodes.note: A curved interface sustains excess pressure: $$\Delta P = \sigma\left(\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$, giving $2\sigma/R$ for a drop and $4\sigma/R$ for a soap bubble (two surfaces). Smaller bubbles are over-pressured more.

nodes.label: Bubble Coalescence
nodes.note: Two soap bubbles merging into one release surface energy, which becomes sound and heat: $$\Delta E = \sigma \Delta A_{total}$$. For a cluster of $n$ drops coalescing, $\Delta A = 4\pi r^2 (n - n^{2/3})$.

nodes.label: Angle of Contact
nodes.note: Young's equation balances the three interfacial tensions: $$\sigma_{SA} = \sigma_{SL} + \sigma_{LA}\cos\theta$$. $\theta < 90^\circ$ (water on glass) gives a concave meniscus and capillary rise.

nodes.label: Force on a Sliding Wire
nodes.note: A soap film on a U-frame pulls the slider with $$F = 2\sigma L$$ (two surfaces). Equilibrium balances this against an applied load plus the film's weight.

nodes.label: Capillary Depression
nodes.note: A non-wetting liquid like mercury is depressed: $$h = \frac{2\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g r} < 0$$ since $\theta > 90^\circ$. The same Jurin formula, with negative h, covers it.

nodes.label: Jurin's Law
nodes.note: Rise in a clean wetting tube: $$h = \frac{2\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$$. Narrower tubes lift the column higher, inversely with radius.

nodes.label: Tube Too Short
nodes.note: If the tube is shorter than $h$, the liquid rises to the top and flattens its meniscus so that $\frac{2\sigma\cos\theta'}{r} = \rho g L$; it does not overflow. The contact angle adjusts instead.
